vibration: something moving quickly back and forth
sound wave: the travelling squeeze of air that carries sound
eardrum: the tiny skin in your ear that trembles with sound
pitch: how high or low a sound is
volume: how loud or soft a sound is
microphone: a tool that catches sound and turns it into a signal

Close your eyes for a moment and just listen. A car outside. A voice in another room. Your own breathing. Even in the quietest place, sound is almost never truly gone. We live inside an ocean of sound, so used to it that we forget it is there at all.

image.note: A child with eyes closed in a room, faint sound-lines coming from many directions

pages.text: But what is sound, really? You cannot see it, hold it, or keep it in a box. Yet it can make you laugh, warn you of danger, or move you to tears. To understand it, we have to look at something you cannot see at all: the air itself.

image.note: An invisible air made faintly visible as tiny drifting dots around a child; curious

pages.text: Every sound begins with something shaking. Pluck a string and watch it blur as it trembles. Bang a drum and feel the skin buzz under your hand. Speak, and put your fingers on your throat, and you will feel it quiver. All sound starts with something moving quickly back and forth. We call that a vibration.

image.note: A hand on a throat feeling it vibrate; a plucked string blurred; a drum skin trembling

pages.text: When the drum skin pushes out, it squashes the air just in front of it. When it pulls back, the air stretches out again. Push, pull, push, pull, very fast, and the air passes this squeezing along, like a shove travelling down a packed queue of people. That travelling shove in the air is a sound wave.

image.note: A row of people passing a shove along; beside it, air being squashed and stretched in bands

pages.text: This is why sound needs something to travel through. Usually that something is air. But sound travels through water too, which is how whales sing to one another across the sea. It travels through solid things as well, often even better. Press your ear to a table and tap the far end, and you will hear it clearly.

image.note: A child pressing an ear to a long table while another taps the far end; discovery

pages.text: And here is a strange truth. In space, where there is no air at all, there is complete silence. A rocket could explode right beside an astronaut and make no sound whatsoever, because there is nothing for the wave to travel through. No air, no sound. Sound cannot cross empty space.

image.note: An astronaut in silent space, a soundless flash nearby; total stillness

pages.text: Sounds differ in two main ways. The first is how high or low they are. When something vibrates very fast, we hear a high sound, like a whistle or a tiny bird. When it vibrates slowly, we hear a low sound, like a big drum or a lorry engine. Fast shaking, high note. Slow shaking, low note.

image.note: A small whistle with fast tight wave-lines; a big drum with slow wide wave-lines

pages.text: The second way is how loud or soft a sound is. A big vibration, with the air pushed hard, makes a loud sound. A tiny vibration makes a soft one. That is why hitting a drum harder makes it louder: you are shaking the air more strongly. Loudness is simply the size of the wave.

image.note: The same drum hit softly (small ripples) and hard (big ripples); the child grinning

pages.text: So how does all this reach your mind? Your ear is beautifully made for catching sound waves. The curved outer ear funnels them inside to a tiny tight skin, your eardrum, which trembles exactly as the drum did. That trembling passes through tiny bones, the smallest in your whole body, into a place full of fluid.

image.note: A clear cutaway of the ear: outer ear, eardrum, tiny bones, spiral inner ear; labelled simply

pages.text: Inside there, thousands of tiny hairs wave in the moving fluid and turn the shaking into signals your brain can read. In less than a blink, a vibration in the air across the room becomes a sound inside your head. Your ears are turning air movements into meaning, all day long, without you asking.

image.note: Tiny hair cells waving in fluid, sending sparks toward the brain; wondrous, small-scale

pages.text: Once people understood that shaking makes sound, they learned to shake things on purpose, beautifully. A drum shakes a skin. A flute shakes a column of air inside a tube. A guitar shakes strings of different thickness, each humming its own note. Every instrument in the world is really just a clever way of controlling a vibration.

image.note: A Nigerian talking drum, a flute, and a guitar together; a small band of children playing

pages.text: The oldest instrument of all needs no wood or string. It is the human voice. Deep in your throat, two small folds of skin vibrate as air rushes past, and your mouth shapes the sound into words or song. When you sing, you carry the very first instrument humans ever had, and you were born already holding it.

image.note: A child singing, throat and mouth shown gently, sound-lines rising; joyful

pages.text: For most of history, sound vanished the instant it was made. A song, once sung, was gone forever. Then people invented ways to catch it. A microphone turns a sound wave into a signal that can be stored, copied, and carried anywhere. Now a voice can be saved for a hundred years, or sent across the world in a moment.

image.note: A voice note being recorded on a phone and arriving on another phone far away; modern life

pages.text: So the next time you send a voice note, or your favourite song fills the room, remember the whole hidden journey. Something shook. It squeezed the air. The wave raced out, was caught, was carried, and finally shook a tiny skin deep inside an ear, and became sound again. All of that, just so you could listen.

image.note: A child smiling, listening to a voice note through earphones, faint wave-lines flowing in; warm, closing
